case_info.scenario: A healthy 25-year-old female presented with an 8-month history of a painful right mandibular lesion (Figure 1A). The patient reported progressive persistent pain and enlargement of the lesion since it was first noticed. She denied any facial trauma history and had no sensory deficits in the inferior alveolar nerve distribution or signs of infection such as purulent discharge, foul taste, warmth, or erythema of the overlying skin. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.

B, Coronal view of maxillofacial computed tomography (CT) showing a multiloculated lesion at the right mandibular angle. The lesion is expansile in nature and located inferior to inferior alveolar nerve. It demonstrates cortical invasion involving both the buccal and lingual aspects.
case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. She had multiple prior emergency department encounters for this lesion, and maxillofacial computed tomography revealed a multiloculated radiolucent lesion situated below the inferior alveolar nerve at the right mandibular angle (Figure 1B). On clinical examination, there was firm, tender external swelling of the right gonial angle along the inferior border. Intraoral findings were unremarkable, with no drainage or evident expansion into the retromolar trigone. An incisional biopsy was performed via a transoral approach. The intralesional content appeared to be dark brown and spongy. A portion of the tissue was sent for frozen section analysis, which revealed the presence of multinucleated giant cells and spindle cells but was nondiagnostic. A fluorescence in situ hybridization study was subsequently performed, confirming a positiveUSP6gene rearrangement.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.

case_info.explanation: An aneurysmal bone cyst (ABC) is a benign lesion most commonly arising in the vertebral column and the long bones, with a higher incidence in the first decades of life and a female predilection. Rarely, ABCs involve the head and neck region, making up 2% to 3% of cases, with the mandible being the most affected site. The exact etiopathogenesis remains unclear, with proposed theories including trauma, vascular anomalies, genetic predisposition, and circulatory disturbances. ABCs may occur as primary lesions or in association with other bone pathologies, such as ossifying fibroma, chondroblastoma, solitary bone cyst, giant cell tumor, and osteoblastoma.1 ABCs are classified into 3 types. The vascular type, which is most common, presents with rapid onset of painful swelling and expansile mass, often associated with pathological fracture and substantial intraoperative bleeding. Histologically, it shows blood-filled spaces separated by fibrous septa containing fibroblasts, osteoclastlike giant cells, and reactive woven bone.2The solid variant, as in this case, develops gradually, manifesting as firm swelling with mild pain. Microscopically, it demonstrates a predominance of fibroblastic proliferation with scattered giant cells and osteoid formation, while cystic blood spaces are few or absent. The mixed type combines features of both.3 ABCs can be difficult to diagnose because of overlapping radiographic and histological features with other primary bone pathologies. ABCs often present as expansile, lytic lesions with septations and cortical thinning, and may demonstrate fluid-fluid levels on magnetic resonance imaging, though not pathognomonic. Osteoblastoma commonly resembles ABCs initially but matures to mixed radiolucent-radiopaque appearance with calcification. In comparison, central giant cell granuloma (CGCG) typically appears as a fusiform radiolucency with variable cortical erosion, a pattern that is radiographically indistinguishable from osteitis fibrosa cystica, also known as brown tumors.4Notably in this case, odontogenic pathology was not considered in the differential because these lesions generally arise above the inferior alveolar canal and are tooth associated. A comprehensive diagnostic approach with laboratory testing and biopsy confirmation is essential. Laboratory studies aid in distinguishing brown tumors, characterized by elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone.5Conventional histology usually suffices to diagnose osteoblastoma, characterized by trabeculae of woven bone lined by active osteoblasts.6However, fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis may be required to distinguish ABCs from CGCGs when conventional study is inconclusive. About 70% of primary ABCs demonstrateUSP6rearrangements (Figure 2), while CGCG may harbor variations in genes such asLRP1BandNOTCH4.7,8 ABCs can be managed through various treatment approaches. The preference is toward surgical excision whenever possible due to its high rate of complete healing and relatively low risk of recurrence. In recent years, there has been growing interest in less invasive options. Percutaneous sclerotherapy with agents such as doxycycline or polidocanol has shown promising results. Other modalities, including embolization, bisphosphonate therapy, and radiotherapy, may also be considered in select cases.9 In conclusion, accurate diagnosis of ABCs is essential, as management strategies differ substantially. ABCs are aggressive lesions typically treated with curettage, surgical excision, sclerotherapy or embolization, whereas brown tumors improve with management of hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, CGCGs, depending on the subtype, may respond to intralesional corticosteroids or denosumab in addition to surgical excision.10The patient in this case is doing well after surgical resection and alloplast jawline reconstruction without issue and is currently 1 year out from surgery without evidence of disease recurrence.
